text:
GPT-6 Astra has cracked *another* German WWI radio message encrypted with ADFGVX.

This message, "RICHI-240", has a single known key, but, to my knowledge, was never cracked by humans before.  My guess is that humans never solved this message because it has 20 characters *missing* for reasons unknown: the "240" in "RICHI-240" signifies that there should be 240 characters in the message, whereas in fact there are only 220.

For purposes of cracking this cipher, the big problem is that it's not clear *where* these characters are missing from, because the order of the characters in the message is scrambled using the key.  Thus, inserting the characters into the message in even slightly the wrong place leads to utterly nonsensical results.  

All this was no problem for GPT-6 Astra, which tried the key with various combinations of hypothetical places from which the characters could have been missing and scored the resulting blocks of text using patterns common in the German language. Relatively early on in the process, this approach rendered coherent German text!  Inserting the 20 missing characters as a string between the 4th and 5th lines of text in the message worked!

The message reads:

AN O H L
11 ARMEE
ALPENKORPS RAUM PETERREVE VERBASZ
21? 21? ? RDD LINIE NAGYBESSKEREK VERSECZ
VERSECZ VON SERBEN BESETZT

The three question marks you see are numerical digits, which cannot be restored by decryping (all we know is that they are three different digits from the following set: 5, 6, 7, 8, 9).  And so, Astra was forced to check its results against historical WWI records.  This search unearthed a French intelligence telegram, which described the situation in the area on November 11, 1918 and identified the German 217 - 219th infantry division and 6th Reserve Division in the area.

Plugging in this missing information, we get the final result:

AN O H L
11 ARMEE
ALPENKORPS RAUM PETERREVE VERBASZ
217 219 6RDD LINIE NAGYBESSKEREK VERSECZ
VERSECZ VON SERBEN BESETZT

Or, in English:

TO SUPREME ARMY COMMAND
11TH ARMY: 
ALPINE CORPS IN THE PETERREVE-VERBASZ AREA.
217TH - 219TH DIVISIONS, AND 6TH RESERVE DIVISION ON THE NAGYBECSKEREK-VERSEC LINE.
VERSEC OCCUPIED BY SERBS.

Astra checked the official history of the Serbian city of Vršac (Versec in Hungarian, and Werschetz in German) and found that, on November 10, 1918, German troops left the city and it was occupied by Serbian forces.  RICHI-240 was sent at 3:38am on the following day to the German Supreme Army Command, informing them of this fact.

11,000 comments asking where to buy. You refreshed Shopify every ten minutes for three days.

$700. Total.

The video worked. You picked the wrong wallet.

THE PRODUCT

A habit tracker aimed at teenage girls. Viral by any definition. 16,000 sessions hit the store. Conversion rate: 0.3%.

The people typing "I need this" did not have a card to type into the checkout.

A near-identical product pointed at men over 40 with thinning hair and a paycheck did $10,000 to $20,000 a month on the same content style.

Same tools. Same format. Different buyer.

THE MATH ON THE SAME VIEWS

16,000 sessions × 0.3% × $15 average order = $720.

Now the adult version. Same 16,000 sessions × 1.5% × $80 = $19,200.

Nothing about the video changed. 26x from the audience alone.

THE DEMAND RATIO

Comment counts lie unless you check them against views.

> 100,000 views: under 4 buy-intent comments is weak, 10+ is strong

> 500,000 views: under 8 weak, 15+ strong

> 1,000,000+ views: under 10 weak, 20+ strong

Buy-intent means "where do I buy this," "link?", "how do I get one." It does not mean "I like this." Those are different sentences.

One buy-intent comment with 40 likes under it outweighs ten scattered ones. The likes are people who wanted it and could not be bothered to type.

THE TWO-MINUTE FILTER

Before you order a single unit, click into 10 of the profiles behind the buy comments.

> Age. Accounts that read as 13 do not convert. Their parents are not in the comments.

> Country. Some markets have never converted for anyone. Views from them count as zero.

Two minutes. Changes the entire read on the product.

THE ONE THAT LIED

A water-chest product. Millions of views. A wall of "link link link." Test order came back: 2 sales.

A branded version was already sitting in big-box retail. A similar wrist product had already flopped for someone else. Two facts outside the comment section beat millions of views inside it.

THE ONE THAT TOLD THE TRUTH

Ankle brace. 800,000 views. 34 buy-intent comments, several with 40+ likes, from adult accounts in strong markets. Well above the 20-per-million bar. Test order confirmed it. About $2,700 per mill.

Less hype. More money. That is usually how it goes.

Run your own version on the video you are about to copy:

> Views on the top video

> Buy-intent comments only

> Likes stacked on those comments

> Age and country of 10 commenters

> The meme trap: the comments talk about the joke, never the product. 6.6 million views, about $100 in sales, creator never posted again.

> The broke audience: your $700 above. A looks-maxing product did 10 million views and $3,000 total for the same reason.

> The unbelievable result: full head of hair in 90 days. The comments say "no way" and the conversion rate drops on an 8 million view video. Fix the timeline in the video, not the product.

> Burner brain: copying whatever is viral without asking why it converts.

> The 3-day quitter.

Virality is a number. Revenue is a different number.

You just paid a month to learn the difference. Do not pay it twice.

🚨 STOP ASKING AI TO “SUMMARIZE THIS PDF.”

That’s barely 10% of what you can do.

🤯 You can use AI to extract insights, find hidden problems, compare documents, build reports, create study material, and make decisions.

Here are the most powerful PDF prompts. 👇

10. Fact-Check the PDF

Prompt:

"Act as a skeptical fact-checking assistant. Analyze the claims made in [PDF] and classify them as directly supported by evidence in the document, reasonable interpretation, unsupported claim, potentially misleading statement, or information that requires external verification. Do not assume a claim is true simply because it appears in the PDF. Create a verification checklist for the claims that matter most."

A solo Shopify operator just laid out his exact setup for running a store on $20 of Claude and pulling $10,478 in profit off $19,100 in monthly revenue. 

No team, no VAs, no agencies.

The math he opens with is the point. Running a store the "real" way costs $150 per product for a copywriter, $600 to $800 a month for a support VA, and $1,000 to $1,500 a month for a media buyer. Over $2,000 a month in overhead before a single person clicks Buy. It's why most stores die in month three.

His version: $20 Claude, $39 Shopify, six prompts.

He calls the six prompts his desktop. Each one does a job a human used to charge for.

research finds a recurring, annoying problem nobody has clearly solved yet. Priced $29 to $79, no single brand owning search results, before/after obvious in 5 seconds of silent video. The prompt forces Claude to cite sources or label every claim "[ASSUMPTION, verify]" so a guess never gets passed off as a fact.

supplier reads reviews like a detective and returns GREEN / YELLOW / RED / UNKNOWN with quoted evidence for every red flag. His first store died from a bad supplier. The product was fine, the shipping wasn't, disputes piled up, the payment processor froze the account. Now no supplier gets an order until this ten-minute check clears.

angle takes competitor listings and their 1 to 3 star reviews and finds the position none of them occupy. "Add reviews" and "better photos" are banned answers. If the complaint is "took 25 days," his page says exactly when it ships, in bold, near the top.

page rewrites AliExpress descriptions in the voice of a friend recommending something they actually use. Two versions, A/B tested. Any sentence that could appear on any product page for any product gets flagged and rewritten.

ad writes a 30-second vertical script as a 4-row shotlist with the exact words spoken. Banned phrases include "game changer," "you need this," "POV," "this changed my life." He films three versions in one evening changing only the first three seconds, runs each at $15/day for 48 hours, kills the two with weak hooks.

sunday runs every week for twenty minutes. Paste the numbers, get told what's broken in the first sentence, no encouragement, no "normal for this stage." Calculates break-even ROAS so he knows whether he's making money or burning it.

Three more prompts get added once sales exist. A post-purchase email flow that quietly brings in a fifth of monthly revenue with no extra ad spend. An offer prompt that raises AOV through bundles priced so margin goes up, not down. An iterate prompt that reads ad results and derives the next batch of hooks from what won, instead of testing more random angles.

Six to ten hours a week on the whole thing. Month one basically broke even. The store doesn't change, the prompts just get better at their jobs.

The line worth stealing: everyone has the same $20 access to Claude. The person making nothing and the person making a few thousand a month are using the identical tool. The difference is who stopped being the bottleneck on every decision in their own business.

text:
WEST BENGAL BYPOLL: THE QUESTIONS AROUND THE ELECTION PROCESS

https://t.co/JmHRGZ6jYq

Senior advocate and Rajya Sabha MP Kapil Sibal has raised serious questions about the Election Commission's handling of the forthcoming Nandigram and Rejinagar Assembly by-elections in West Bengal.

The Election Commission froze the All India Trinamool Congress name and its “Flowers & Grass” symbol on September 17, directing the rival factions to contest the by-elections under separate names and symbols. The bypolls are scheduled for 6 October 2026. 

Sibal argues that the timing of the EC's intervention deserves scrutiny because the electoral process was already underway. In his press conference, he also discusses the subsequent withdrawal of the Mamata faction's Nandigram candidate and the arrest of Congress candidate Milan Pradhan shortly after Mamata Banerjee announced support for him. 

Independent reporting confirms the sequence: Sanchita Pradhan Dey withdrew her nomination on September 18; Mamata Banerjee subsequently announced support for Congress's Milan Pradhan; Pradhan was then arrested in connection with pending cases dating back to the 2007 Nandigram land-acquisition agitation. He was later remanded to judicial custody. 

The most important issue here is not which political faction one supports.

It is whether electoral institutions inspire confidence among all participants and voters.

The Election Commission says its interim decision was intended to place the rival factions on an even footing while their dispute over the party's identity remains unresolved. 

Sibal sees the same sequence differently and alleges that the timing and conduct of the process raise questions about institutional accountability. Those are his allegations, not established judicial findings. 

That distinction matters.

Because in a democracy, the credibility of an election does not depend only on the final result.

It also depends on whether citizens can reasonably believe that the rules were applied transparently, consistently and without partisan preference.

And when controversial decisions occur immediately before a poll, the demand for transparency becomes even more important.

Institutions must not merely be independent.
They must be seen to act independently.

The question therefore is simple:

Can India's electoral institutions command public trust if their most consequential decisions remain surrounded by unanswered questions about timing, procedure and accountability?

Russia is running an active influence operation targeting the 2026 midterms. That part is documented. The more important story is what comes after the disclosure.

Start with the detection problem. The Election Threats Executive Group is gone or effectively gutted. The interagency coordination machinery that existed in 2020 has been stripped down. So the operation is running into an environment where the early-warning architecture is weaker than it has been at any point since 2016. Disclosure happened through journalism, not through government detection and public attribution. That is a meaningful shift. It means the response timeline compresses badly, because by the time reporting confirms a campaign, it has already been running.

Now look at the tradecraft evolution, because that is what actually matters for the next eighteen months.

The 2018 operation required large human operator teams to generate volume. The 2022 operation was more efficient but still recognizable by the signature of coordinated inauthentic behavior: accounts moving in lockstep, posting at patterns that don't match organic human activity, translated idioms. The 2026 operation is documented as using AI-enhanced content generation. What that means operationally is smaller teams producing more content at higher quality with fewer of the linguistic tells that platform trust and safety teams trained their detection on. The old detection signatures are degrading in usefulness. The platforms have not yet published updated detection frameworks that account for this, and several of them have reduced the teams that would build those frameworks.

The targeting is also worth watching closely. The reported focus on suppressing Democratic voter enthusiasm and turnout is consistent with a shift away from the 2016-era strategy of broad polarization for polarization's sake. The 2026 targeting is more surgical. Economic anxiety and cost-of-living narratives are being used as the entry point. That is smart operational design. Those narratives are grounded in real conditions. They don't require fabrication to land, they just require framing. A voter seeing content that says their grocery bill is high because of Democratic governance isn't necessarily seeing a lie. They're seeing a selective frame delivered at scale by a foreign actor with a stake in the outcome. That's much harder to counter than a fabricated story about a candidate, because the counter-argument doesn't begin with "that's false."

The demographic micro-targeting piece deserves more attention than it's getting. The reporting notes that the operation identifies specific demographic segments susceptible to particular narrative framings. This is not novel in concept, but the AI-enhancement of content generation means the operation can now produce tailored content for those segments at a scale and speed that wasn't achievable in 2018. A Black voter in Georgia, a union household in Michigan, a young male voter anywhere who has migrated to platforms with lighter moderation: each of those segments gets different content, built to land differently. The operational overhead of that kind of targeting has dropped significantly. Which means the targeting will get more granular, not less.

The platform environment is a structural problem that isn't going to resolve before November 2026. Reduced trust and safety investment at the major platforms, combined with altered content moderation philosophies, means the coordinated industry response that characterized 2020 is not the baseline assumption anymore. In 2020, platforms were investing heavily in this, coordinating with each other and with government, and still running removal operations in the weeks before the election. That infrastructure has been partially dismantled. The Russian operation in 2026 is landing into that changed environment intentionally. The timing is not coincidental.

What defenders should actually be watching:

Platform-level detection of coordinated behavior will be slower and less comprehensive than in 2020. That means the operational window for the Russian campaign is longer before meaningful disruption. Watch for whether any of the major platforms publish transparency reports on influence operation takedowns in the six months before the midterms. The absence of such reports will be informative.

The journalism-based disclosure model that surfaced this operation is going to be under pressure. Investigative reporting on foreign interference is expensive, slow, and often legally complicated. Without government attribution to anchor the reporting, outlets have to build the case independently. That is harder, and some operations will not get disclosed on a timeline that is useful for voter awareness.

The use of authentic American political grievances as raw material is going to make legal and regulatory responses nearly impossible before November 2026. Content that is factually selective but not fabricated sits in a gray zone that neither platform policy nor federal law handles well. Expect the operation to stay in that gray zone deliberately.

State-level election officials are not well-resourced to fill the gap left by the federal infrastructure reductions. The Election Assistance Commission has limited authority. The FBI field offices that would normally handle threat communication to local officials are operating in an environment where that kind of proactive engagement has become politically complicated. The result is that the people running the actual mechanics of the election in competitive districts will have less threat-relevant information than they had in 2020. That is a real operational advantage for the Russians, and it compounds over time.

One thing that isn't discussed enough: the Russian operation does not need to change vote totals to succeed. Measurable success metrics for this kind of campaign include reduced turnout in targeted demographics, increased distrust in electoral institutions, and the amplification of post-election disputes regardless of outcome. All of those outcomes are achievable without touching a single voting machine. The campaign is already running. Some of those effects are already accumulating.

The question for the next eighteen months isn't whether the operation exists. It's whether the detection and attribution infrastructure that was stripped back can be partially reconstituted, whether platforms will invest in disclosure even in the absence of government pressure to do so, and whether journalists can maintain the bandwidth to surface operations that government is no longer reliably surfacing. Right now the answer to all three is uncertain, which is exactly the operating environment Russia planned for.

India has quietly frozen Starlink. It issued the license nearly a year ago, then let the final security clearance sit, and the whole satellite-comms sector has slowed with it. This is not a compliance dispute. New Delhi is asking a question Starlink can't really answer: given its US ownership and global network, how can it promise to follow Indian rules when Washington wants the opposite?

Notice the tell. Jio and Bharti get an easier ride because their satellite partners are European, not a US-controlled operator. The worry isn't the satellites, it's whose hand is on the switch. And it lands days before SpaceX's IPO at a $1.75tn valuation, with Starlink as the main revenue engine, a reminder that the global rollout is far from uniform: shut out of China, and now stuck in India too.

Tesla and Starlink have sought entry into India for years. Tesla was blocked by a 110% tariff and local manufacturing rules, while Starlink faced national security concerns.  

With Trump back, things have turned into a cakewalk for Elon. The EV import tariff dropped from 110% to 15%, opening doors for Tesla, and Starlink is also making inroads. This seems to be a result of diplomatic arm-twisting rather than mutual benefit.  

Still, I see a blessing in disguise wrt Tesla, especially for consumers. High tariffs are primarily imposed to help domestic manufacturers grow and make the country self-reliant. We gave a lot of space for Tatas, Marutis, Mahindras, etc., to grow, innovate, and dominate, even at the cost of Indian consumers paying to protect substandard products and keep out competitive alternatives.  

If local manufacturers still can't compete, so be it. The entry-level Tesla will cost less than 40 lakh and has much better specs, performance, range, and battery life than any domestic EV. Why should Indian consumers be denied that when even Chinese companies are selling cars in India?  

Starlink, however, is a potentially risky deal if not diligently regulated, primarily due to the threat to our digital sovereignty. If its per-consumer cost is lower than Jio's and Airtel's current rates, local ISPs will be wiped out, creating a duopoly. If Jio and Airtel shift much of their traffic to Starlink, we’d be at its mercy, Musk could cut off our internet, suppress counterviews, and ban users at will. He could also refuse to block content harmful to national security.

Have you noticed this?

A lot of things don't become expensive overnight.

First, they're free. Then you start using them regularly. Then, somewhere along the way, you start paying for them without thinking twice.

We've seen this happen everywhere in India-

Jio gave us ridiculously cheap data.
We stopped thinking twice before using it.

UPI made digital payments effortless.
Now the ecosystem around payments is becoming a business opportunity.

Food delivery apps gave us free delivery and heavy discounts.
We stopped calling the restaurant. Then came delivery fees, platform fees and all the other little charges.

OTT platforms started with cheap subscriptions and free trials.
Now every cricket match, movie and series seems to have its own platform.

Banks gave us zero-balance accounts and free services.
Over time, minimum balances, ATM limits and various service charges became normal.

The interesting part isn't the charge. It's the timing. Nobody wants to pay for something they don't use.

So first, get them to use it. Then use it often. Then make it convenient. Then make it a habit. And only then put a price on it.

It's not a new trick. Product, technology, generation, everything else changes.

But, the sequence has remained remarkably consistent:
Free → Habit → Dependence → Monetisation.

Sometimes, the smartest price is ₹0 at the beginning.

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

IFF statement on Delhi Police notices to Meta seeking the identities of creators, and the continuing removal of CJP protest content from Instagram

19 September 2026

Over the course of today, several content creators who posted about the Jantar Mantar protests have written to us after receiving an email from Meta. The email states that Meta Platforms Inc. has received "a valid legal process seeking information about your Facebook account", that it "intends to comply with the request… to the extent consistent with applicable law", and that the information sought "may include basic identifying information associated with the account". The requesting party is the Delhi Police. The email does not say under which provision the request has been made, in which FIR, for what offence, or by which officer. This is not the first request of its kind. On 27 July the Delhi Police directed platforms to remove content uploaded during the protests, and on 29 July it wrote to X seeking the names, addresses, phone numbers, email IDs and login and logout records of accounts which it said had posted "derogatory, malicious and defamatory" material about the Prime Minister.

These requests come at the end of a long process of removal which has been concentrated on Instagram, the platform on which the protest was organised and reported. Sakhi, the Jamia student whose "vastegune huia" reels went to millions, found in early August that four reels uploaded between 20 and 25 July had been restricted in India with the standard notice citing a notice from "The Government of India/Law Enforcement under section 79(3)(b)". These included a video of Delhi Police personnel unloading food from a truck after the lathi charge and an interview with Mohammed Junaid, a volunteer who distributed food at Jantar Mantar. A fifth reel, in which Sakhi described how their clothes were torn during the police action on 20 July, was removed on a different ground altogether, Instagram's community standard on "adult sexual exploitation". Gopika, the vice president of JNUSU, uploaded a screenshot of a rape threat she had received along with a note about it, and the post was removed for "sexual and nudity content". The SFI's video of Junaid was taken down under "legal requirements". Gajendra Singh's footage of a protester injured on 20 July was restricted the next day.

The same pattern is visible at news organisations. Maktoob Media's two videos on the crackdown were blocked within minutes of upload by what Instagram described as an automated system acting under the IT Rules, with no route to appeal. Scroll, The Hindu, Alt News and Peek TV have each reported posts on pellet injuries, on the doxxing of women protesters and on police conduct being restricted in India. Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka of the CJP and Arvind Kejriwal have reported the same. In every case the user who clicks "See why" is told that the action was taken "based on a local legal requirement" and nothing more. Some restrictions apply to whole accounts and not to individual posts. 

In a matter in which IFF assisted before the Delhi High Court, a creator's verified account with about 1,03,000 followers was withheld across India on the basis of a single-page, system-generated notice from a State police CID which named no post and no complainant. On 18 September Instagram restricted a post by the Software Freedom Law Centre which discussed the removal of Alt News' fact-checks. A reel on the proposed data centre in Visakhapatnam, which IFF also challenged, was restored this week after three and a half months, after the blocking order obtained in litigation turned out to allege "misinformation" about a person who does not appear in the reel. It is also worth recording that this has taken place in the weeks after Meta, having removed a post by the Prime Minister and been given three days by a parliamentary committee to apologise, sent its chief global affairs officer to Delhi to do so.

The case of the journalist Ila Kazmi shows how the system works when it is directed at reporting on the police themselves. On 23 July she published a two-part report on her Instagram account @ ilareports showing police personnel seated in a van at Jantar Mantar and matching live CCTV footage against photographs of individuals. This was the first public documentation of facial recognition being used at the protest, and IFF relied on it when it wrote to the Commissioner of Police and filed RTIs. Part 2 of the report was restricted in India on 24 July under a Section 79(3)(b) notice. On 4 September she posted a reel referring to The Indian Express's investigation into the list of 2,873 persons which the Delhi Police told the Supreme Court its facial recognition system had flagged at the protest. By the police's own preliminary assessment, 162 people on that list were lodged in prison at the time. On 9 September her entire account was withheld in India, again citing Section 79(3)(b), even as the Account Status page on the same app informed her that her account "meets all of our guidelines". She wrote to MeitY. On 15 September the Section 69A Cell of the Ministry replied that the account "is blocked under section 79(3)(b) of the IT act" and that she was "requested to take up the matter with the concerned State department". The reply does not say which State or which department. The Union ministry which administers the blocking framework has confirmed to a journalist that her account has been blocked and has declined to tell her by whom. IFF is assisting her.

Most of the people who have written to us are not employed by news organisations. They are students, freelancers and people who run one account with a few thousand followers, in some cases a lakh. They have no lawyers and no way of reaching Meta other than an in-app form which produces the same message each time. When such an account is withheld its audience disappears at once. When its owner receives an email of the kind described above, they do not know what it is or what will follow from it. It is these accounts, more than the larger outlets, which have borne the removals since July and which are now being asked to give up their identities.

IFF condemns the demand for the identities of persons who documented, satirised or commented on a public protest, and the removal of the record they created. We call on the Delhi Police to withdraw the notices and on Meta to decline to act on them and to restore the content.

On the law, there is no investigation for these notices to serve. 

On 1 September 2026, on the application of the Delhi Police itself, the Supreme Court invoked Article 142 to quash all thirteen FIRs registered in Delhi over the protests of 20 to 25 July "along with any proceedings arising therefrom". It directed that any other FIR concerning the same incidents "shall not be pursued or investigated" and shall be "taken to have been closed for all intents and purposes", and it barred the registration of any fresh FIR save one against 2,873 named individuals, confined to allegations of bodily harm and destruction of public property. 

The order records the acknowledgement of the Union and the States that "mere participation in the protests is not taken as an offence under the penal laws", and it makes the relief conditional on both sides honouring the commitments made before the Court. A notice served on an intermediary under Section 94 of the BNSS or Rule 3(1)(j) of the IT Rules is a step in an investigation, and it must be tied to one which the law permits. The Delhi Police is not the investigating agency in any of the thirteen quashed FIRs, which suggests that these requests arise from a separate FIR concerning posts about the Prime Minister. That FIR concerns the same incidents and stands closed by the order. 

In any event defamation under Section 356 of the BNS is a non-cognisable offence, and a court may take cognisance of it only on the complaint of the person aggrieved under Section 222 of the BNSS. The police have no power to investigate it of their own motion, let alone to collect the identities of those who may have committed it.

Our demands

1. The Delhi Police must withdraw every notice issued to an intermediary seeking the identity or subscriber details of any person in connection with content about the protests of 20 to 25 July 2026, and must disclose the FIR, the provision and the officer under whose authority each such notice was issued.

2. The Ministry of Home Affairs and MeitY must publish every notice issued under Section 79(3)(b) concerning content about the protests since 20 July, withdraw those directed at satire, commentary and documentation, and inform every affected person of the agency which issued the notice against them, beginning with the account @ ilareports

3. Meta must decline to act on legal process which, on the face of the Supreme Court's orders of 28 July and 1 September, has no lawful investigation behind it. It must supply to each user it has notified a copy of the process served on it. It must restore the posts, reels and accounts restricted in India since 20 July, inform each affected user of the agency and the ground on which the restriction was imposed, stop applying community standards to documentation of protests and police action, and publish figures for the notices and data requests it has received from Indian authorities since July.

4. The surveillance of protestors, through facial recognition at the site and through requests for data from intermediaries afterwards, must be placed before the Supreme Court and the HPEC. IFF will assist affected persons in doing so.

Any person who has received such an email from Meta, or whose posts, reels or account have been removed or withheld in India, can write to us at legal@internetfreedom.in. We are providing assistance on a pro bono basis.

I have been ill from lead and mercury and demolition dust but also extremely disabled from whistleblower retaliation by the city of Philadelphia. Many hospitalizations, especially from PTSD—I think I need a federal lawyer. The problems with Krasner made me write a small bit of the horror I have been through for 20 years now. Beyond your scoop I am sure. 

I sent evidence to Krasner to get a port-conviction review for Sean Benschop—who has been in jail for the demolition accident at Market Street, June 5, 2013.

My troubles with the construction project adjacent to my house that cracked my hours and poisoned me with lead and mercury were doing demolition with no permits—among other permit failures. I have a copy of that violation that led to the shutdown.

By the time of the Markert Street demolition, I knew a lot because I spent years going to meetings and learning safety regs and sending the city's very own safety regs to the city. I got to know top people in city planning very well, and they knew me. Including the deputy mayor Alan Greenburg, who is also big at city planning.

Around the fall of 2011, we were both at a symposium presented by the Public Interest Law Center that featured Vernice Travis Miller, who worked on a demolition protocol in Baltimore in conjunction with Johns Hopkins, covering the health aspect of demolition.

In 2006—soon after I was ill from both the demolition dust and lead and mercury from the site next to my house (by 6 feet)—I attended a meeting in the Northern Liberties neighborhood that was organized by Hilary Regan. The feature speaker there was also presenting the same Balitmore demolition safety protocols. Many city officials were at that meeting, mainly from city planning and licenses and inspections, and Department of Environmental Protection.

We were all given the Balitmore demolition safety protocols. One of the first things in that publication was "REMOVE EVERYONE IN THE ADJACENT AREA BUILDING NEXT TO ACTIVE DEMOLITION."

The same Manuel and other person who worked on the Baltimore protocols was presented at the Fall 2011 symposium. I was there, and Alan Greenburger—the deputy mayor—was there. Everyone got a copy of the safety protocols.

Just before the symposium, the police came to my door-- a tempplace I was living because I could no longer live in my house, where I had become the target of many crimes, and the local police had been informed to never help me—plus the poor air quality that continually put me in a hospital.

So the police came to my door and showed me an email I had Alan Greenburger tell him about the meeting on demolition safety and related topics presented by the Public Interest Law Center. The police asked me if I had written the email and if I was going to the meeting. I said yes, I had paid for my ticket, and there was no reason why I should not go.

Police at my door asking about me going to this meeting??!!

I went, and Alan Greenburg showed up and sat up front next to the featured speaker, Vrenice Travis Miller, and interacted with her verbally. I have the court reporter transcript of that meeting so I can prove that.

I was always polite at meetings, and I said nothing at that meeting—except during a break. I politely turned to another person—most were lawyers—and told her a bit about my situation. She was hostile and said nobody was ever going to help me. Later, I found out that one of their top lawyers had something to do with that land next to my house—but I don't have sure evidence, so I will not say—but that organization in many ways has sabotaged all along.

About that same month a woman died in a flood that a retired water engineer pointed at the project next to my house and said the building on top of the creek that was under that land was a flood danger. At the 2006 meeting, I brought the stream map and showed City Planning the same thing and told them it was a danger. One dead.

Then deputy mayor Alan Greenburger spent a couple of months emailing (I have some copies of those) back and forth about the Salvation Army and the demo project. He was the professional. He had the safety protocols about not doing demos next to any building with people in it. He had been hearing about demo danger and all the other dangers for years from me. ALL HE HAD TO DO WAS ORDER SOME WARNING SIGNS PUT UP AND SOME BARRIERS ON THE SIDEWALK TO SAY DANGER.

He did not—so a bunch more people died that day. And later on national TV, Mayor Nutter, surrounded by a group of city officials, many of whom I had talked to about my demo and lead and mercury problems—including Alan Greenburg—stood together, and Mayor Nutter told the world on national TV that Philadelphia did not know much about demolition.

I gave all this info to Krasner and asked for a post-conviction for the demolition driver who was obeying orders from his boss. I had heard Krasner was into post conviction.  But obviously, freedom is only for real hard-core murderers, not someone set up as a scapegoat for the higher ranks of the PHILADELPHIA GOVERNMENT.

Mahatma Gandhi once said that if this country is to progress in the right direction and to prevent its democracy from becoming the democracy of goons, young people must go to the villages and live there to serve.

After independence, people from Gandhian, Sarvodaya, progressive, and leftist ideologies have gone to villages to do service work.

These people work to organize villagers, remove superstitions, make them aware of their rights, and help with agriculture, health, and education.

In the village of Shukravaasa, Parvatpura Panchayat, in Dewas district of Madhya Pradesh, a group of young men and women are living in the village, making people aware and organized.

Among these youths are engineers, doctors, journalists, and filmmakers.

Because these young people are spreading awareness about democracy, the Constitution, and related matters, tribal people associated with their committee have started contesting elections for the Panchayat and Legislative Assembly.

This has angered the local people in power and political parties.

A short while ago, the police misbehaved with and assaulted these youths.

When these young people tried to hold a press conference against the attack, members of the Bajrang Dal—right in the presence of police and media—again assaulted them and stopped the press conference from happening.

An FIR was filed against their colleague Saurabh Banerjee for religious conversion, and he was illegally kept in police custody for 2 days. After that, he was kept in police remand for 7 more days, and then, without any evidence, he was sent to jail.

The most alarming thing this time is that the police filed an FIR against them for religious conversion.

Bajrang Dal’s allegation is that these people are making tribals into atheists.

If you read the FIR, the allegation is:

> “I greeted Saurabh by saying Ram Ram and asked what work he had. Saurabh replied, ‘What is this Ram Ram? Ram and Sita were brother and sister; they are not gods.’ Pressuring me, he said, ‘Hindu gods and goddesses are made of stone; what will happen by worshiping stone? God doesn’t exist at all, and you too should stop believing in God.’
After hearing this, I drove him out of my house. Saurabh has also made such provocative statements against Hindu gods and goddesses to other villagers before. Today, I told my father, Kamal Singh, about this, and he called other villagers—Nilesh Patel, Ravi Rawat, Manoj Patel, Brahmanand Chaudhary, Sunil Meena, and Vikas Parihar—and explained everything. Everyone suggested going to the police station to file a report.
Saurabh Banerjee has hurt our religious sentiments. Kindly register an FIR against Saurabh Banerjee.
Signature in Hindi: Petitioner Sachin, son of Kamal Singh Bamaniya, Village Shukravaasa, District Dewas, Date: 26.07.2025.”

According to Section 299 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, the anti-conversion law applies when you force someone to change from one religion to another through inducement or fear.

First of all, in the Indian Constitution, atheism is not a religion.

So, the anti-conversion law cannot even apply.

In India, there are millions of people like us who are atheists, and every day we consider atheism a scientific understanding. We try to tell everyone that God is an imagination, God cannot solve your problems—you must struggle yourself.

Will the Bajrang Dal tomorrow break into our homes, beat us, file FIRs against us, and make atheism a crime in this country?

Are we becoming a Hindu Taliban, where a blasphemy law is implemented, and under its name, speaking about superstition, blind faith, and promoting scientific thinking is declared a crime?

In Madhya Pradesh, the youth had set up a center for their organization, which the Madhya Pradesh government has now demolished with a bulldozer.

Tribals have come before the media and said that these people have never converted anyone’s religion.

But the Bajrang Dal and the police are intimidating the tribals and fabricating false cases against these young social workers.

If the police were to read the 22 vows of Babasaheb Ambedkar—the architect of our Constitution—they would put him in jail too, because in them Babasaheb made people pledge not to believe in Hindu gods and goddesses.

- Himanshu Kumar

Hey everyone and @SamsungIndia Story start from 23 April 2026 till today, I have been trapped in what feels like a complete service scam by Samsung’s authorized service centre in Dharampeth, Nagpur, Maharashtra.

I discovered a sudden issue in the 0.6x ultra-wide camera of my Samsung Galaxy S25 Ultra. The phone was never dropped, never mishandled. After researching online, I found MANY users reporting the exact same issue with the new 50MP ultra-wide sensor. Reddit, YouTube, Samsung Community — same problem everywhere.

Because my device was out of warranty, the Dharampeth service centre immediately gave me a ₹4000 quotation instead of acknowledging a possible manufacturing defect.

After endless emails, Samsung support kept repeating: “You have to pay.”

Why should customers pay for Samsung’s hardware failure?

After getting exhausted, I posted on X on 26 April tagging Samsung Electronics India. Only then did they react. Customer Experience Manager Kajal contacted me, and after I shared proof from multiple users online, Samsung finally offered a 73% discount.

I accepted because I was mentally tired of fighting.

On 6 May, I submitted the device. On 7 May, I collected it after paying ₹1000.

Camera fixed?
YES.

New disaster?
BACK PANEL STARTED COMING OFF THE VERY NEXT MORNING.

I informed the service centre on WhatsApp. They ignored the messages.

Visited again on 11 May — they “fixed” it.

Two days later?
BACK PANEL AGAIN COMING OFF.

Visited again on 14 May — this time the behavior became shocking.

Instead of accepting poor repair quality, staff started accusing ME of removing the back panel with sharp objects. They checked the device and found ZERO evidence.

Then they saw BGMI installed.

And suddenly their excuse became:
“BGMI is a third-party app. Using third-party apps voids warranty and service.”

Imagine buying one of Samsung’s most powerful flagship phones and being told GAMING can void service support.

When I asked for a written denial letter, they REFUSED.

When I started recording for proof, they stopped answering questions and began ignoring me completely.

I had no option left except calling the police.

ONLY after police intervention did the entire attitude of the service centre change. Suddenly:
“We never denied service.”
“We are ready to repair.”

They even requested police officers to convince me to delete the videos I recorded.

After another repair attempt, they told me:
“Do not use BGMI for 12 hours.”

I followed everything they said.

Result?
BACK PANEL STARTED COMING OFF AGAIN.

Since then I have been continuously emailing Samsung support and Kajal from customer experience, asking for a permanent solution or replacement because I cannot travel 13KM repeatedly for the SAME ISSUE.

Today again, after being told to visit the service centre, they AGAIN accused me and AGAIN refused service while refusing to provide any written denial.

The moment I started recording, everyone went silent.

This is the reality of Samsung’s “premium flagship experience” in Nagpur.

Customers are blamed.
Manufacturing defects are ignored.
Poor repairs are repeated.
Written denials are refused.
And consumers are forced into endless visits until they give up.

Absolutely shameful. @SamsungMobile @SamsungIndia 

#Samsung #SamsungIndia #GalaxyS25Ultra #SamsungService #Nagpur #ConsumerRights #scamservice

text:
Tuesday 15 September 2026.🔺⚙️🛠️🔺🌐
The World Clock — Worldwide https://t.co/GgjvZlg7Zf
Source: Tass*com
Information warfare has no rules, creating them is our next step — GFCN president
Vladimir Tabak, president of the Global Fact-Checking Network
© Danil Aikin/TASS
Interview with Vladimir Tabak, president of the Global Fact-Checking Network

President of the Global Fact-Checking Network (GFCN) Vladimir Tabak told TASS in an interview ahead of the Dialogue about Fakes 4.0 forum about where most information attacks against Russia originate, how a disinformation campaign targeting elections to the State Duma is being prepared abroad, and which issues that are particularly sensitive to Russians are currently most vulnerable to fake news.

– Today we will be discussing a very important problem which, like a terrible disease, is capable of poisoning and replacing reality itself – fake news. And my first question to you is: which areas of Russians’ lives are being attacked by this disease first and foremost?

– It seems to me that today there are no areas that have escaped this disease. But if we are talking about the areas that are most vulnerable to it, those are everything related to security, political processes, and social issues. We know that there are currently certain fuel-related difficulties in the regions. There are also a large number of phishing websites offering fake fuel coupons, as well as unverified websites with completely bogus maps of gas stations that were created simply to collect users’ data. This is a vivid example of how a situation arising offline can prompt the creation of projects of this kind, which can then pose a fairly serious threat to citizens themselves and to the state, because systematic efforts against the country as a whole begin to take shape.

– When you hear all of this, it is hard not to feel a sense of hopelessness. Is there really nothing we can do to protect ourselves from this problem? Is there no antidote? Perhaps you could name some of the most effective methods of countering fake news?

– The situation with fake news is quite complicated today. We understand that there is a huge amount of cyber fraud. For me, even regardless of where I work, when 'a Sberbank representative' (a fake representative of Russia’s largest bank) connects you over the phone to 'an FSB representative' (a fake officer from Russia’s Federal Security Service), that is a somewhat strange situation. (This is a common scam tactic designed to gain the victim’s trust by making the call appear official – TASS). Or when an 'FSB representative' calls you on a video call, sitting in his office, and presents you with some kind of accusations.

But a huge number of people actually fall for this. On top of that, technologies are developing. There are deepfakes, for example. Today, 64% of people in surveys conducted by Dialogue Regions say that they know what deepfakes are. There were, of course, fewer of them before – 59% as of September 2025. At the same time, 80% overall say that they encounter unreliable information. What does that tell us? It tells us that we can focus exclusively on raising the population’s level of media literacy, creating an ecosystem of trust, and beyond that, it will still come down to personal responsibility, apart from situations where law enforcement agencies need to step in afterward. But at the moment when a person encounters one piece of information or another, the responsibility ultimately falls on the user.

This does not change the fact that we need to package and deliver our own information quickly and accurately. We need to be able to debunk disinformation that is spreading widely among a broad audience. In this sense, the state should not absolve itself of responsibility for, so to speak, organizing a large-scale process of informing people, debunking false information, providing education, and working with government agencies so that they, too, understand how to counter this. But given the scale at which this kind of information is being disseminated today, the only thing that can counter it on such a mass scale is a high level of media literacy and, ultimately, a basic degree of critical thinking on the part of users about what they are reading.

– The explosive growth in the amount of fake news has been driven by the development of artificial intelligence (AI). And there is currently a debate in many countries about mandatory labeling of content. Do you consider this a necessary measure? Perhaps you are in dialogue with government authorities or other organizations on this issue?

– At some point and to some extent, all countries will regulate this type of content. In fact, there are already pilot examples of countries where such content is being regulated. What is very important here is to find the right balance, because we understand that there are two opposite poles. At one end, AI helps reduce production costs and makes it possible to create content more quickly – it serves a positive function. And that function definitely should not get lost behind this bureaucratic process. At the other end, we have those same tools being deliberately used for destructive purposes. Here we need to find that delicate balance which, on the one hand, will allow legitimate content producers to continue operating in this market without unnecessary restrictions and, on the other hand, will create the right foundation for systematically countering those who use these technologies to cause harm.

Read also
From trendy toys to tools of political manipulation: rapid advancement of AI avatars
But the production landscape has also changed dramatically, if we can call it that. We understand that previously, this kind of content was primarily produced by small specialized groups, those who were themselves engaged in developing artificial intelligence. Today, technologies have reached a level at which this product has become mass-market, meaning that more than 50–60 percent of AI-generated content, for example, that you see on the internet is content created by users themselves. So, to answer the question you asked, a decision to introduce content labeling is inevitable in the foreseeable future.

– In a few days, we will have an important event – elections to the State Duma. This is probably a period of particularly high vulnerability to fake news. Are you seeing preparations for a disinformation campaign coming from outside the country? Through which channels, perhaps, are they planning to spread fake news, and what narratives will they target?

– There are classic approaches to delegitimizing the electoral process. These include videos related to the voting process itself. Even without taking any particular technologies into account, this could mean, for example, using old videos. I will give the most basic example: staged videos filmed at a polling station in order to convince the viewer that what they are seeing is happening here and now. This will certainly happen; we understand that.

Read also
False mobilization claims put society on edge ahead of Russian elections — GFCN chief
But there are also narratives that have nothing to do with the voting process itself – narratives intended to make this period more difficult for the authorities and for the country. And perhaps the most striking fake news story in this regard is the story about mobilization, which does not directly affect the elections. It could have an impact if mobilization were actually announced. But rumors about it undoubtedly create significant tension both among certain segments of the population and in society as a whole. And so, as you can see, even at the highest level, the Russian president addressed this issue, because the information really did spread extremely widely.

Obviously, there are opinion polls and there is analysis, but there is also a simple rule you can see in any personal chat group: if people you know start actively discussing a particular topic, then you know that topic is genuinely on people’s minds. I can say that this was discussed in every personal chat I am part of, and at every meeting I attended, someone asked a similar question. And it is clear that those who created and injected this fake news were relying on the idea that during the previous period, there was still a certain segment of people who became frightened and left, as well as the parents of those people, who were themselves under considerable stress. So, the objective pursued by our opponents is clear. I would identify this as one of the most prominent narratives we are observing.

– If it is possible to trace the source and, for example, make a list, a sort of tier list, of which countries carry out the most information attacks against Russia, what objectives are these countries pursuing?

– Ukraine is in first place, but this is fairly easy to explain. We are in a state of armed conflict, and today information warfare is part of the larger war. So, it would be strange if we were now talking about other countries dominating Ukraine in this regard. Ukraine has a separate unit, the Center for Information and Psychological Operations, or CIPsO, which is part of the regular armed forces and is classified as a military unit.

This is visible across many different issues. In other words, they get involved in any crisis-related topic and try to escalate it as much as possible and create additional tension around it. But at the same time, we understand that there are a number of countries that are also behaving quite aggressively and using specialized institutions to operate against us. First and foremost, this is Britain. This is a country that behaves quite aggressively in the information sphere. There are different methods. They have, so to speak, verified sources – media outlets and platforms that they support through various grant systems and through direct funding. There is also work involving AI, work targeting specific segments of the population, ranging from simple tactics in which certain issues are injected into the information space to more sophisticated operations.

But despite the fact that we are currently at a fairly acute stage of information confrontation, we should not discount ordinary people who often spread unreliable information without having any malicious intent. Again, this brings us back to the issue of cognitive awareness. Our task is to stop constantly saying that everything we see is somehow a product of our adversary. That is not the case. Fake news existed before. People tend, especially in situations when they feel uncertain or do not know the answers to questions that concern them, to come up with rather strange answers themselves, to put it politely, or to seek those answers in completely unverified sources. So here we need to work with the broader public so that people learn to verify information.

– So, what is needed is broad-based educational and explanatory work?

– Yes.

– Now let us talk about the association that you head. The Global Fact-Checking Network was established in 2025. Can you give us an interim assessment of this period? How has the nature of your activities, the scope of your tasks, and the scale of the network changed?

– First of all, I believe that the project has worked out overall. It is important to understand that this was initially a voluntary initiative. The project was created by us, by Russia’s News Agency TASS, and by the New Media Workshop. We created it amid the publicity surrounding our lawsuit against the FBI in the United States after we were accused of allegedly interfering in the US elections. And, to be completely honest, initially it was something of a PR move. But various industry participants from different countries showed interest, and today we have more than 125 journalists in the Association from 55 countries.

And every time at the forum (referring to the Dialogue about Fakes 4.0 forum – TASS), more and more speakers and participants from different countries attend. The total number of guests at the forum has already exceeded 2,000–3,000, including Russian participants, but a significant share still comes from different countries, including countries that are currently considered unfriendly, yet there are journalists and media professionals there who are willing to engage with us.

We have released a number of interesting and high-profile investigations, and we have developed a substantial educational program. Several memoranda have been adopted at major international events based on the GFCN Code of Responsible Fact-Checking. Some provisions of our Code were also included in the final statement of the 12th BRICS Communications Ministers’ Meeting at the recent summit in India. And today we have begun working quite closely with colleagues from China and Kazakhstan. A GFCN expert was in Kazakhstan during the elections as part of the CIS observation mission, and before that our representatives were in Venezuela. Again, we are invited to participate in various events, and it is important to understand that GFCN currently has no funding of any kind. In other words, we are essentially participants and members who have other, primary jobs, and for whom this is, as our opponents like to put it, a "guilty pleasure."

So, as a project created entirely on enthusiasm, I think the Network has exceeded my expectations in any case. On about five or six occasions already, the International Fact-Checking Network, a fact-checking association funded by the Poynter Institute, has mentioned in its articles that we are a lying Kremlin propaganda network. I consider that a great success. So, when I compare the resources invested with the results, I am very pleased with the work of the Network.

– We have already mentioned information adversaries. As allies, as I understand it, you have named China and Kazakhstan?

– There are actually many countries. We are currently integrating closely with the Organization of Asia-Pacific News Agencies (OANA), which is currently chaired by TASS Director General Andrey Kondrashov. So this includes Asia, the Pacific, Latin American countries, and CIS countries. Some show greater interest, others less. We are as open as possible here. We have an educational section on our website, which already contains more than 170 articles and videos covering various areas of fact-checking, media literacy, and OSINT tools (open-source intelligence research – TASS), all of which are available to users on the website. Our position here is quite open. We are not claiming ideological leadership; rather, we want to bring together people who are interested in this field. So, some countries show more active interest, and there are individual representatives of countries who are particularly active. But I would say that as this issue becomes increasingly relevant, interest will continue to grow.

– You have touched on the Network’s educational role. In your view, what qualities need to be cultivated among young journalists, fact-checkers, and researchers? What do you pay particular attention to, and what are you trying to develop?

– There is an expression: an inquisitive mind. I think that is the most important thing. I was personally the driving force behind launching this initiative, but I am not an OSINT specialist (a professional who collects, analyzes, and interprets information from publicly available sources – TASS) and I am not a fact-checker (a professional who specializes in verifying the accuracy of information – TASS) myself. What matters to me is creating a certain atmosphere for this "community" and giving it an opportunity to grow. And when I look at people who, in my view and in the view of my colleagues, have that kind of fact-checking talent, they are extremely inquisitive. They are meticulous, perhaps even somewhat distrustful at times, but I think people like that could work very well in law enforcement agencies.

I am exaggerating a little, of course, but you need to be appropriately skeptical. We are not talking about some kind of blind or irrational distrust. You need to start from the assumption that we live in a very difficult information environment filled with millions of unverified sources. At the same time, the internet now gives us the ability to verify an enormous amount of information without resorting to any closed or restricted verification methods. The ability to think critically on the one hand and to use these tools on the other, taken together, gives us an excellent synergy for helping these talented people grow and develop.

– From everything we have discussed, it already seems that fact-checking has ceased to be primarily a tool for journalists. Can we say that it has now become a distinct international area of cooperation? And what kind of global model for interaction would you perhaps propose?

– It is difficult for me to say what a global model of cooperation would look like, but I have thought, for example, about the fact that there are conventional rules governing warfare. If those rules are violated, there is a regulatory body where sanctions or consequences for such actions are considered. For example, is inducing a teenager to commit murder or arson as part of information warfare essentially the same thing as using cluster munitions in a conventional war? I believe it is. Because that goes beyond the bounds of information confrontation in the sense in which I see and understand it. And in my view, even if today we are talking about us and our adversaries with whom we are waging this information war, there still need to be certain rules. Unfortunately, as of today, there is no such framework for defining those rules. It would be quite difficult to establish it at the global level right now. We understand the geopolitical situation, especially if we were, so to speak, the ones initiating such an effort. But in my view, these rules need to emerge. And that is the next step.

But globally, despite all the popularity and hype surrounding fact-checking, it has still not become a fundamental part of journalism. And we need to understand that journalism itself has also undergone a transformation. As a graduate of the journalism faculty at Moscow State University, I can say that journalism today and journalism even 15 years ago are completely different fields, and today many major publications are facing the question of how they can continue to exist, because modern media consumption and the monetization of platforms that results from it seem not to provide for their presence on anything close to the same scale.

So, the question here is not how fact-checking will be incorporated into journalism; the broader question is what will happen to journalism itself in the coming years. And fact-checking, in my view, is not purely a journalistic field. At a basic everyday level, it is something that every adult today should possess at least minimal skills in for their own safety. At the professional level, it involves groups of ordinary people who work in the interests of private companies, in the interests of the state, and in their own interests, if they are investigators or people working in related fields.

– I will be completely candid: it is very interesting to listen to you, and it makes me want to delve deeper into these issues. On September 22, we have a major event coming up – the Dialogue about Fakes 4.0 forum, which will provide an opportunity to discuss all of this in greater detail.

– Yes, we will have presentations there, and we are very grateful to the Russian Foreign Ministry for supporting the forum throughout all these years. Without the Foreign Ministry, we certainly would not have been able to put together an event on this scale. And this year, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Viktorovich Lavrov will personally take part in the forum. We are very grateful to him for responding to our requests. And we are also grateful to Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Vladimirovna Zakharova for her endless, consistent support.

– This is the fourth time the forum has been held. What will make this year special? What topics will be the key ones?

– I do not like talking about any particular forum as being special, because then we somewhat diminish the value of the previous forums that came before it. In my view, the community is simply becoming larger, stronger, and broader. Again, new international projects of a higher level are emerging, and negotiations with a number of countries are also moving to a new level. For me, this is a way to formalize agreements – in some cases in an official setting, in others in an informal one – and once again to draw centralized attention to the issue that my colleagues at "Dialogue," our partners, and I have been working on for several years now.

– And what are you expecting in terms of scale?

– Every year, our forum is larger than the previous one. And this year we will have more participants than we did last year. So, in terms of scale, yes, it will be bigger. But the issue is not the number of participants; first and foremost, we look at the level of representation and the standing of the experts taking part. text:
"They could have killed my son": Mother demands answers

A Montreal man was pepper-sprayed, kicked, dragged across the pavement,  and stabbed by a group of masked men near Place-des-Arts, an attack that  left him with a punctured and collapsed lung, broken ribs and severe  facial fractures.

A 24-year-old man is speaking out after a brutal attack by more  than ten men of colour near Place-des-Arts metro station in downtown  Montreal left him hospitalized with serious injuries.

For security reasons and out of fear of retaliation, Rebel News is protecting the identities of both the victim and his mother.

Montreal police confirmed that a robbery involving multiple  suspects occurred on August 26. According to police, the victim was  pepper-sprayed, beaten and stabbed with a sharp object.

The victim told Rebel News he had been with friends near the  metro when a group of roughly two dozen masked individuals appeared  nearby. He described them as dressed mostly in black and said, “They  were all wearing COVID masks to hide their faces.”

Later that night, he says the group approached him from behind.

“One of them put his hand on my shoulder. He pulled me around, and immediately I… I got hit in the face with pepper spray.”

What followed, according to the victim, was a prolonged and vicious beating.

“Then they started punching me, kicking me, and dragging me  along the ground by my bag,” he said. “During that, I was stabbed  several times in the chest area, in the back.”

One stab wound punctured his lung. “Air was going in and out through my back. And I didn’t even know I’d been stabbed.”

He says his lung later collapsed and doctors had to remove both  air and blood before reinflating it. He also reported broken ribs,  facial fractures and continuing problems with vision in his left eye.

His approximately $5,000 Louis Vuitton bag, phone, cards and keys were stolen. Perhaps most disturbing to the family is what allegedly happened around them.

“It affects me quite a bit,” the victim said after being asked  about bystanders and friends who did not intervene. “I would at least  have intervened.”

His mother remains shaken. “Oh my God! I was angry, I was devastated, and I was worried,” she said after seeing video of the attack.

Asked about safety in Montreal, her answer was unequivocal: “There is no safety in Montreal anymore.”

Police have told Rebel News that no arrests have been made so far.

Women talk a lot about misogyny, eve teasing, and harrasement. I agree. Those things happen a lot.

But such things happen with men too. Men just don't speak about it. Because if they do, either it's disregarded in the assumption that he must have liked it, or he is mocked.

I want to speak about it. 
Here are some instances from my life. 

1. Year 2019. Chennai Airport. I was in boarding queue of Air India, when a random woman put her hands across my shoulder to take support. No consent. No asking. She just did it. Probably she thought why would a man object if a woman touches him. Modesty is only for women. I had to tell her to remove it. 

2. Year 2017. This was in a flight from Mumbai to Delhi. I had pre-booked the window seat. The woman in the middle seat asked for it, as she didn't want to sit in between two males. I refused. She retaliated with, "Madarchod, seat book kar liya to tere baap ka ho gaya." I wasn't very good with Hindi then, but I understood she was abusing me. Anyway, I put back my earphones and ignored her. 

3. Year 2022. Bangalore - Koromangla. I was standing outside an apartment to meet my friend. A woman was coming out in a hurry with a trolley. She stumbled. Was about to fall head on, on the ground. But I grabbed her arm to prevent her from falling. It was an automatic reaction. Her trolley tilted and it's handle hit my crotch hard. Her first reponse was, "How dare you grab me?" I told her you were about to fall. She said, she wasn't going to fall. She called me a pervert and hurried off. I was left there, holding my balls in pain. The guard and I looked at each other. We conveyed with our eyes what we didn't speak in words.

4. Year 2012 - Italy (Rome). I was on a solo trip to Europe. A tourist lady was asking people for the way to Pizzeria Ristoro. She was speaking Spanish and people couldn't understand it. I knew Spanish, so I thought I will guide her as I had been there a day before. Google maps weren't a rage back then. She gave me a big peck on the cheeks, hugged me tight, as a way to say thanks. She had a horrible breath coming out of her mouth and nose. I felt disgusted from within. Her intention wasn't bad perhaps, but she didn't respect the boundary.

5. Year 2026 - Sri Lanka. This was the funniest of all. I was playing catch with my son in a park in Nuwara Eliya. There were a group of women sitting close by. A berry from the tree above fell on one of them. She thought I hit her with something. She created a scene. There were a few policemen standing nearby who quickly came over. Thankfully, my wife was recording me and my son playing catch and she showed the video where the falling berry was recorded. That lady said, "Asshole" and left. My wife was about to retaliate, but the police said to just let it go. There was no point. Ah, those ladies, looking for cues of harrasement everywhere.

These are just a few top of the mind. There are other incidents too which I don't even remember clearly. I just let it go because there is no point in fighting.

If a man retaliates, it can even backfire. Because the woman can fabricate a story of her own, make herself look like the victim and the police then won't even listen to the man's version.

Do you have any stories?
Feel free to share.
